name: Agriculture and commodity trading
systems: Grain and ag-retail accounting ERPs for elevators and cooperatives: AGRIS (Greenstone/Cultura, PC 1984, Windows 2000-03), Agvance (SSI, 1981 origin, Windows mid-1990s), AgTrax/TraxView (1996), Merchant Ag (Ever.Ag/EFC), AgVision, Primetics, AMIC, CORETech (Cultura/Constellation portfolio)

Commodity trading and risk management (CTRM) for traders and processors: ION Openlink Endur, ION TriplePoint (Triple Point Technology, 1993), ION Agtech, ION Allegro, Softmar (chartering), iRely i21 (successor to older iRely origination/grain products)
Large-enterprise ERP estates at global merchants (e.g. ADM worldwide ERP programme), often with SAP Commodity Management
Workarounds around the core: spreadsheets for analytics and non-physical trades, email/paper for post-trade execution, paper books at palm-fruit dealers
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The core is 1980s-90s Windows client-server rather than mainframe, and its vendors keep modernising it in place (SQL, hosted versions) while overlays like Bushel and Covantis work around it. That makes the category less locked-in on platform and skills than mainframe-heavy categories. The paper, email and spreadsheet workarounds are more severe than typical.

s1.why: Primary vendor histories show the leading systems in both tiers predate 2005 as on-prem PC/Windows client-server. AGRIS was a grain elevator accounting system in 1981, went to PC in 1984 and to Windows in 2000-03, with SQL added only in 2014-16. Agvance (SSI, founded 1981, Windows suite mid-1990s) reports 3,800+ ag retail locations and about 50% of the CropLife Top 100, which shows it dominates. On the CTRM side, TriplePoint (1993) and Openlink Endur (1990s) are also pre-2005. Caveats: none of this is mainframe or IBM i, and Agvance has offered a cloud (SKY) version since 2016, so part of that base is now hosted.

s2.why: The only primary evidence is one firm. ADM's 10-Ks show a worldwide ERP and legacy-system replacement still 'in phases over the next several years' from FY2016 through FY2024, with no deployments in 2024. That is a general ERP programme at a single top merchant. The Adaptive CTRM case study ('extended period of time') is an anonymous vendor case. I found no evidence of 7+ year contracts or of typical replacement timelines for the dominant grain accounting systems (AGRIS, Agvance, AgTrax) or for CTRMs across the category.

s3.why: There is quantified evidence that the dominant players work around their systems with email, paper and re-keying. Consensys, citing FAO/IPPC ePhyto, says more than 275M emails a year are exchanged to process about 11,000 ocean grain shipments, and the six largest merchants formed Covantis to cut rekeyed entries. An Eka/Quoreka survey found 66% of commodity firms rely primarily on spreadsheets for analysis versus 12% on CTRM, and an agri CTRM case study retires an Excel-based solution for non-physical trades. Caveats: the Eka survey is a vendor survey of only 50 executives across ag, chemicals and energy, and the Covantis reduction figures are projections. The email-volume figure is the strongest single datapoint.

s4.why: The only support is a specialist recruiter (Cititec), who describes a 'small pool' of people who know E/CTRM systems, and a Capco consultancy paper on Endur implementation skills. Both lean toward energy trading, and both are secondary or self-interested. I found nothing on skills scarcity for AGRIS, Agvance or other grain accounting systems, and no COBOL/RPG angle, since no midrange grain system was confirmed.

reasons_to_stay: Grain accounting systems embed scale-ticket, contract, settlement, warehouse-receipt and patronage logic tied to local regulation (e.g. USWA licensing, farmer tax exemptions), so replacement means rebuilding compliance-critical workflows

Global merchants' ERP/CTRM replacements run for years in phases (ADM: FY2016 to FY2024 and still not finished), with material control risk (ADM's FY2024 10-K reports a material weakness in internal control and no ERP deployments that year)
Vendors keep modernising in place (AGRIS added MS SQL in 2014-16, Agvance added the SKY cloud version in 2016), which lowers the pressure to switch
Consolidated vendor ownership (Constellation/Volaris via Cultura; ION across Openlink, TriplePoint, Allegro and Agtech) keeps products supported long-term
Integration overlays (e.g. Bushel integrates with existing grain accounting systems instead of replacing them) extend the life of the legacy core
Scarce specialist implementation skills (Endur and E/CTRM) raise project risk and cost

name: Airline reservations and passenger service
systems: IBM ACP / TPF / z/TPF mainframe transaction platform (origin of PARS/IPARS reservation applications)
Sabre host reservation system (American Airlines/IBM, built 1960, live 1964) and its airline-hosted successor SabreSonic Customer Sales & Service
Amadeus Altéa Suite (Reservation, Inventory, Departure Control), hosted PSS for full-service carriers
Navitaire Open Skies (1994, HP3000) and New Skies (conversions from 2005), LCC PSS now owned by Amadeus
Travelport (Worldspan/Galileo/Apollo) z/TPF hosting of airline internal reservation systems (Delta, United, Northwest historically)
SITA Gabriel (Unisys-based) and SITA Horizon PSS
Videcom VRS (UK, regional/small carriers)
Radixx (LCC PSS, Sabre-owned since 2019)
Airline in-house legacy PSS (e.g. ANA domestic system operating since 1988)
Cryptic / green-screen agent terminals and Sabre Scribe scripts layered on the host
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Less legacy-locked at the runtime than a typical enterprise category, because the two dominant PSS vendors (Amadeus by 2018, Sabre mostly by 2024) have already moved their own hosts off the mainframe and run them as multi-tenant hosted services. More locked at the contract and data-model level than most: a vendor switch is a multi-year, airline-wide cutover through IATA PNR, EDIFACT and interline plumbing.

s1.why: The dominant hosts all came from mainframes. Sabre was built on IBM mainframes from 1960 and went live in 1964. Amadeus Altéa ran on the Amadeus TPF complex: Qantas went live on Altéa Reservation in 2002, and Amadeus did not retire its TPF mainframes until 2017-2018. Navitaire Open Skies launched in 1994 on HP3000. Primary sources from both main vendors confirm this: Sabre's FY2025 10-K says its platform 'evolved from mainframe-based transaction processing', and Amadeus has published its own account of retiring TPF. Caveat for the study: those same sources show the dominant installed base is no longer on mainframe. Amadeus has run fully on open systems since 2018 and is moving to Azure. Sabre moved about 90% of its workloads to Google Cloud by Feb 2024. What is legacy today is the application lineage (PNR and EDIFACT data models, cryptic command interfaces), not the runtime.

s2.why: Several primary sources across vendors show multi-year replacements and long contracts. Southwest's own release says its move to Altéa took about 3 years (2014-2017) and 1,500+ people. Qantas moved to Altéa module by module from 2002 to 2008, and signed a 10-year deal in 2007. LATAM signed a 10-year Sabre PSS contract in 2015 and implemented through 2018. ANA plans to replace a domestic PSS that has run since 1988, with migration over FY2025-26. Sabre's 10-K puts hosted airline contracts at roughly 3-10 years with minimum volumes. Even the vendors' own re-platforming took years: Amadeus's mainframe exit took about 2,000 effort-years, and Sabre missed its own 2023 mainframe-exit target.

s3.why: The only concrete evidence is one RPA vendor press release (Automation Anywhere's call-center bot that re-keys refunds and vouchers), which is vendor marketing. There is also anecdotal material on Sabre Scribe and cryptic-command scripting. The DataArt screen-scraping source returned 403 and could not be read, and no evidence of spreadsheet workarounds was found. Cryptic terminal use is a native interface, not proof of a workaround. Nothing quantifies how widespread this is across Altéa, Navitaire or SabreSonic users.

s4.why: IBM's Redpaper does say 'specialized TPF skills can be scarce'. But that is a platform vendor talking about z/TPF, and the two largest PSS vendors have mostly left z/TPF: Amadeus fully by 2018, Sabre about 90% by 2024. Navitaire is .NET and cloud-hosted. For the dominant installed systems, airline staff need Altéa, Navitaire or Sabre configuration skills and cryptic-command fluency, and no source shows those are scarce. The CIO Dive mainframe skills-gap piece is secondary and not specific to this category. Scarcity is real only for the remaining TPF holdouts (some Travelport-heritage hosts, in-house carrier systems).

reasons_to_stay: Cutover risk is existential. A PSS swap touches every booking, ticket and check-in. Southwest needed 3 years and 1,500+ people, and Qantas phased modules over 2002-2008.
Long hosted contracts with minimum annual volume commitments (Sabre: 3-10 years) and exit costs.
Interline, codeshare, alliance and GDS connectivity, and IATA EDIFACT/ticketing/BSP integrations, are built around the incumbent host.
Performance: z/TPF is purpose-built for high-volume seat-inventory transactions, and IBM positions it as unique for airline workloads.
Incumbents are modernizing in place (Sabre moving off mainframe to cloud; Amadeus Nevio offer/order with Finnair, Lufthansa Group, AF-KLM, BA, Saudia). That lowers the urgency to switch vendor.
Agents and airport staff are trained on cryptic commands and scripts, so retraining costs are high.
Revenue management, loyalty, DCS and accounting systems are tightly coupled to PSS data feeds.

name: Capital markets trading, clearing and brokerage back-office
systems: Broadridge Brokerage Processing Services (BPS), the US broker-dealer back office. Its lineage goes back to the ADP brokerage services group (1962), and Broadridge still runs it on mainframe infrastructure that Kyndryl operates
63 moons (formerly Financial Technologies) ODIN broker front-office/trading terminal (India, 1998)
63 moons exchange trading, clearing and settlement stack (DOME framework 2002; MCX platform since 2003)
ASX CHESS clearing, settlement and subregister system (Australia, live since 1994)
NSE NOW broker trading front end (India, discontinued 2020)
MPC (Micro Piranti Computer) S21 / S21+ BOFIS broker back office (Indonesia)
FSS FLEX core securities system (Vietnam)
TCS BaNCS for market infrastructure and brokerage. It is the replacement platform at MCX rather than a legacy incumbent
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more locked in than typical enterprise software. Its cores are regulator-gated network utilities (exchanges, clearing houses, depositories), and every link to them must be re-certified, so failed replacements like ASX CHESS cost hundreds of millions and are public. But the end-user broker layer already has well-funded cloud-native challengers (Apex, Alpaca, DriveWealth, Clear Street), which makes it less locked than core banking.

s1.why: Primary sources show pre-2005 on-prem or mainframe cores for the dominant systems in two major markets. Broadridge's FY2026 10-K says Kyndryl runs its mainframe and midrange operations, with that deal extended to 2031 and a new mainframe lease starting 2027. Broadridge's brokerage processing goes back to 1962 and it serves the 15 largest US wealth providers. The RBA describes ASX CHESS, live since 1994, as a 29-year-old system. ODIN (1998) and DOME (2002) date from the same era. One gap: the SEA cores (MPC S21, FSS FLEX) have no verified ship date.

s2.why: Two national clearing systems have quantified, primary-source replacement timelines. ASX started replacing CHESS in 2016, wrote off A$245-255m in 2022, and the program now runs to about 2029. MCX's move from 63 moons to TCS took from Feb 2021 to Oct 2023, with quarterly extension fees rising from Rs 15 cr to Rs 125 cr, and SEBI fined MCX for the late disclosure. Broadridge's mainframe outsourcing runs to 2031, and it carries $819m of deferred client conversion and start-up costs. One caveat: the strongest cases are market-infrastructure utilities. For broker back offices, multi-year conversions are inferred from Broadridge's deferred costs, not measured.

s3.why: The only evidence is secondary. The TRADE quotes Acuiti's head of research saying most sell-side firms still use spreadsheets, email and chat, but the survey numbers are paywalled and unverified. The evidence is industry-wide and is not tied to Broadridge, CHESS, ODIN or any named core. No source shows re-keying or screen-scraping against a specific dominant system.

s4.why: The one primary source covers a single system. The RBA (confirmed) says ASX has significant key-person risk on CHESS because of the skills the ageing system needs, including its programming language, and that vendors had not announced support plans past 2025. Nothing comparable was found for Broadridge BPS, ODIN or the SEA back offices. General COBOL-scarcity figures come from modernization vendors, not from this category.

reasons_to_stay: Regulators gate cutover. SEBI asked MCX on 28 Sep 2023 to hold its planned 3 Oct go-live, and the RBA/ASIC oversee CHESS milestones, so switching takes regulatory sign-off and mock trading.
Replacement failure is costly and public. ASX wrote off A$245-255m in 2022 after Accenture found the new software 63% complete. Boards that saw this choose the incumbent extension.

The incumbent gains pricing power during migration. MCX's 63 moons support fees rose from Rs 15 cr to Rs 125 cr a quarter while the TCS platform slipped, and staying still looked safer than a rushed cutover.
Conversion costs are sunk and multi-year. Broadridge carries $819m of deferred client conversion costs amortised over service terms, and clients would face the same cost again to leave.

Network integration: a broker back office links to the exchange, the depository (KSEI C-BEST in Indonesia, VSDC in Vietnam, CDSL/NSDL in India), bank RDN accounts and the clearing house. Every link has to be re-certified.
The current system works. ASX's 2022 release said current CHESS remains secure and stable and is performing well.

But cloud processors (Marqeta, Thredd, Pismo, Zeta) have already won the greenfield fintech segment, so the lock-in is concentrated at incumbent banks.

s1.why: The issuer platforms that dominate the installed base all predate 2005 and run on mainframe or NonStop hardware. TSYS TS2 (1994) and VisionPLUS (late 1995, descended from CardPac in 1982) both run on COBOL/JCL/CICS mainframes, and VisionPLUS carries 600M+ cards. FIS BASE2000 is also a mainframe product. ACI's own history page says BASE24 was developed in the mid-1970s for Tandem NonStop, and it had 131 customers by 1986. Fiserv's 10-K confirms that Optis, FirstVision and VisionPLUS are its card platforms. These products span the big three processors (TSYS, Fiserv/First Data, FIS) and the leading switch, not one vendor. Two caveats: the technology detail comes from Mphasis, a secondary consulting blog, and the research's 1982 BASE24 date is wrong (ACI says mid-1970s).

s2.why: Primary filings show multi-year replacements at the largest issuers. Bank of America's 2012 TSYS deal had a six-year minimum term plus a conversion of about 24 months, so roughly 8 years end to end. JPMorgan Chase took a perpetual TS2 license (TSYS 8-K). TSYS 10-Ks say issuer processing contracts generally run three to ten years, with early-termination penalties and annual revenue minimums. Global Payments' 10-K describes the same structure. Two caveats: the 3-to-10-year range does not by itself prove that 7+ years is typical, and the 'usual 30 months' migration time comes from OpenWay's CEO, a vendor. The multi-year conversion prong is clearly met for tier-1 issuers.

s3.why: The only evidence is a marketing blog from Rivero, a dispute-software vendor. It says issuers reconcile Mastercard dispute fund movements with manual spreadsheets and tribal knowledge. That covers one adjacent function (disputes and chargebacks), not the core processing system, and it is a vendor selling the fix. No regulator, independent survey or practitioner study was found showing re-keying or screen-scraping around TS2, VisionPLUS or Optis.

s4.why: The BMC 2025 Mainframe Survey has 45% of financial-services respondents citing staffing and skills as a priority. That covers all financial-services mainframes, not card processing, and the blog gives no sample size. VisionPLUS and BASE24 job posts asking for 8-10 years of experience show the skill is niche, but they are anecdotal and do not prove scarcity. The Mphasis source says nothing about skills. India-based training shops and offshore vendors (Mphasis, Synechron) appear to keep a VisionPLUS bench, so the pool is narrow rather than shown to be shrinking.

reasons_to_stay: Long contracts with annual minimums and early-termination penalties (Global Payments 10-K). The Bank of America TS2 deal had a 6-year minimum term.
Conversions are risky multi-year projects: 24 months for Bank of America, and a 'usual 30 months' for a core card migration per OpenWay.
Mainframe platforms are proven at very large scale (600M+ cards on VisionPLUS versions) with high availability for authorization.
Scheme certifications, regulatory reporting and fraud and collections integrations are built up over decades around the core.
Incumbents are modernizing in place. Fiserv is re-engineering Optis (Celent), which lowers the urgency to switch.
Licensed in-house options (TS2 perpetual license) let large banks keep control without a platform change.

Sage's own KB confirms Sage 300 CRE (Timberline, from 1971) still runs as Windows client-server on the Pervasive/Actian file engine, and Sage advises against VPN because a dropped connection can lock files or damage data. s3.why: The best evidence is the independent JBKnowledge ConTech survey (2019 and 2020). Where construction apps do not integrate, firms move data manually (49-53%) or by spreadsheet (44-48%), and only 5% say all their apps integrate. Accountants are named among the groups that still rely on spreadsheets. The survey covers the industry's whole app stack and does not tie re-keying to Sage 300 CRE, Vista or Spectrum. s4.why: Scarcity is shown only for niche products: a COINS developer post asks for Progress OpenEdge ABL plus day-one COINS expertise, and CGC eCMS is tied to IBM i. The dominant US products (Sage 300 CRE, Vista and Spectrum on Windows/SQL) have a large reseller and consultant channel (Aktion, RKL, Kerr and many regional Sage partners) and hundreds of open job postings. No quantified shortage was found. The scarce skill is product-specific admin and report-writing knowledge, which no source measures.

reasons_to_stay: Job costing, payroll and union/certified payroll are embedded in decades of data. Construction payroll (prevailing wage, union fringes, multi-state) is hard to replicate.
Failed enterprise ERP replacements are well publicised: Kier's Oracle project grew from GBP 30m to about GBP 90m, and Interserve abandoned its rollout with a GBP 17m writedown.
The Trimble Viewpoint, Sage and Access Coins ecosystems sell bolt-on modules and hosted versions, so customers can move to cloud hosting without re-platforming.
Point solutions (Field Materials, Siteline, Briq) sit on top of Vista and Sage 300 CRE, which lowers pressure to replace the core.
Some vendors (e.g. CMiC) still support on-premise deployment, and construction tolerates on-prem more than most industries.
WIP schedules, surety and bonding reports, and auditors' CFMA-style reporting are built around existing report formats.
Thin margins (Vietnam contractors under 10% gross) and cyclical cash flow limit IT budgets.

On replacement duration, the evidence is anecdotal tier-1 cases: CBA took five years and over A$1B (CEO via iTnews), TSB's Proteo4UK cutover failed, and Jack Henry plans a ~15-year rewrite with 10-15 years of IBM i coexistence. A typical US community bank conversion takes about a year. Quantified tenure is strong: 61% of banks have kept the same core provider for more than 10 years (KC Fed), more than a third for 20+ years, and about three quarters stay to avoid conversion (ICBA). That tenure is lock-in, not proof of multi-year replacement.

s3.why: The only primary source is one bank anecdote: the SDNY Citibank/Revlon opinion describes a manual three-field 'wash account' workaround in Flexcube that misdirected about $894M. Survey figures on spreadsheets and manual processes (e.g. Wolters Kluwer's 88% of US lenders using spreadsheets) come from vendors, cover regulatory and risk work, and do not tie the workaround to the core system. No regulator or quantified source shows re-keying or screen-scraping around the dominant cores.

s4.why: Evidence is secondary: a BMC vendor blog citing Reuters (43% of banking systems on COBOL), mainframe-vendor survey claims, and GAO-25-107795, which covers federal agencies, not banks. RPG/IBM i and COBOL skills for SilverLake, CIF 20/20 and Systematics are plausibly scarce. But the large non-US installed base (Temenos T24, Finacle, FLEXCUBE, BaNCS) runs on Java/jBASE/Oracle stacks with deep Indian and SEA talent pools, so scarcity is not shown across the category.

reasons_to_stay: The risk of a failed migration is existential and publicly punished: TSB's 2018 migration led to GBP48.65M in FCA and PRA fines and multi-day outages for 5.2M customers.
Replacement takes years and costs a lot: CBA's program ran five years and cost over A$1B against an original A$580M four-year forecast.
Vendors themselves expect 10-15 years of coexistence. Jack Henry says most customers will keep running IBM i cores for ten or fifteen years and it will keep supporting them.
Outsourced core contracts auto-renew at multi-year terms (Jack Henry's typically run six years; Fiserv cites high renewal rates), and termination fees and deconversion costs build switching friction.

The core is the system of record for deposits, loans and the GL, with decades of business rules held only in code. The Citi Flexcube case shows how much process knowledge sits in manuals and operator habits.
Regulator expectations on operational resilience and outsourcing (PRA/FCA, MAS TRM, OJK, RBI) add approval and testing overhead to any switch.
Integration lock-in: payments, digital banking, cards and regulatory reporting are all wired to the existing core's interfaces.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More locked-in than typical enterprise software, because each jurisdiction is a single sovereign buyer. It works on annual appropriations, has statutory record and judicial-consensus constraints, and depends on many interfaces to police, prosecutors and DMV. Rollouts take a decade. It is less mainframe-bound than banking or tax, since much of the US moved onto 2003-era vendor platforms (Tyler, Journal Technologies) and most Asian judiciaries built post-2007 systems.

s1.why: Primary sources show pre-2005 on-prem cores for the dominant systems in the largest markets. US federal CM/ECF (every federal court, run as localized per-court applications) is 'nearly three decades' old per the US Courts' own 2026 release. Tyler Odyssey, the leading US state-court platform, had general release in Q3 2003 as on-prem client-server (Tyler FY2003 10-K). Germany's Länder systems (JUDICA, EUREKA, forumSTAR, MESTA) predate the 2017 GeFa replacement project (BMJV). UK Libra was procured in 1996-2002 (NAO). Caveats: the Hawaii mainframe detail dates from about 2012 and may be retired, and most Asian systems are post-2005 builds (India CIS 2007, Malaysia e-Kehakiman 2011, PH eCourt 2013, SG eLitigation 2013). So this is strong for the US, UK, EU and AU only, not SEA or India.

s2.why: Several primary sources across separate jurisdictions show decade-scale replacements. Maryland's statewide MDEC rollout ran from fall 2014 to May 2024, which the Maryland Judiciary itself describes as county by county over 10 years. Germany's GeFa started in 2017 and targets 2030 (BMJV). CM/ECF replacement has been studied since the 18F reports and is still in pilot in 2026, with completion two to three years out. HMCTS reform ran from 2016 to 2025 (NAO). Victoria chose Journal Technologies in 2019 and criminal go-live came in 2026. This is a pattern across buyers, not one anecdote. California CCMS ($260m to $1.9bn, then terminated) is seen only in a search snippet.

s3.why: The evidence is real but anecdotal and old. The Hawaii RFP (about 2012, one state) says data passed between DC Crim and HAJIS must be manually re-entered, alongside paper, fax and spreadsheets. Computerworld (2018, secondary) reports Victoria's manual processes on top of nine CMSs. OSR found UK Common Platform staff typing free text instead of result codes, which is a data-quality problem in a new system, not a legacy workaround. No quantified or cross-jurisdiction source shows re-keying or spreadsheet dependence across the dominant installed base (Odyssey, eCourt, CM/ECF).

s4.why: No opened court-specific source shows that skills are scarce. The support is indirect. Hawaii's (about 2012) Adabas/Natural/COBOL-CICS stack, the Georgetown JIF roadmap's general remark that COBOL makes court modernization cost-prohibitive, and general COBOL-shortage surveys (Computerworld) are not judiciary data. The court-specific items (a Courthouse News quote about a retired programmer, the Berrien County COBOL/Natural review) could not be opened, and my search did not surface them either. The dominant current platforms (Tyler Odyssey on .NET, Journal Technologies eCourt on Java/web, CM/ECF on Perl/web) do not need a scarce mainframe skill set. Scarcity applies to the residual in-house mainframe tier only.

reasons_to_stay: Replacements fail or run long and over budget. California CCMS ($260m to $1.9bn, then terminated), UK Libra (£146m bid rose to £318m, core application missed its 2001 deadline), HMCTS Common Platform rollout paused over performance problems
Statewide migrations take a decade or more (Maryland MDEC 2014-2024, Germany GeFa 2017-2030), so courts keep the old system running in parallel for years
Courts depend on many interfaces with police, prosecutors, criminal history repositories, NCIC and DMV (Hawaii lists AG, HCJDC, NCIC, DOT and police interfaces), so every interface must be rebuilt
Statutory record-keeping and data integrity. Common Platform free-text results corrupted official criminal statistics (OSR), which raises perceived risk
Funding is fragmented: Michigan's 242 trial courts have 165 local funding sources. Budgets are annual appropriations, not capital programmes
Judicial independence and consensus. A single judge can stop a modernization project (Georgetown JIF roadmap)
Few vendors and lock-in to incumbents (Tyler, Journal Technologies, equivant) with long statewide contracts

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Hospital EHRs are more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software on age and replacement time: M/MUMPS and 1990s client-server cores, 10-year contracts, and multi-billion-dollar multi-year cutovers. But the dominant vendor (Epic) is gaining share and keeps its skill pipeline fed, so skill scarcity is weaker than in mainframe categories.

s1.why: The three vendors that hold about 80% of US acute hospitals (KLAS 2026: Epic 43.7%, Oracle Health/Cerner 21.9%, MEDITECH 14.7%) all run cores from before 2005. Epic Chronicles is an M/MUMPS database (Epic founded 1979) usually run on-prem or Epic-hosted, and it is not cloud-native. Cerner Millennium is a late-1990s client-server design. MEDITECH dates MAGIC to 1979-82 and Client/Server to 1994, and its 10-K and anniversary page confirm these. Outside the US the pattern repeats: VistA (40+ years), SAP IS-H (1990s), Sunrise at SingHealth (1998), HBCIS (about 1990) and Malaysia THIS (1999). One caveat: Cerner's Millennium ship date was not confirmed from a primary source. Oracle's 2025 cloud EHR is still ambulatory-only.

s2.why: GAO (primary, which I opened) confirms the VA replacement. The IDA estimate is $49.8B: 13 years of implementation plus 15 years of sustainment. Deployments paused from April 2023 to December 2024, and not all centers will be done by the May 2028 contract end. This is a sector-wide pattern, not one case. NHS trusts sign 10-year Epic EPR contracts: Lewisham and Greenwich £52M to 2036, with go-live a year after signing; Somerset and Dorset £222M, 2026-2036. Cabinet Office caps EPR terms at 10 years, so 10 is the norm. Others: Queensland's HBCIS replacement at about 7 years, SingHealth's Sunrise extended to 2029, and SAP IS-H support stretched to 2030/2033.

s3.why: The main source is a peer-reviewed scoping review (Blijleven et al., JMIR 2022), which includes 62 of 737 studies. It documents workarounds such as paper persistence, duplicate documentation and side systems. But it covers EHRs in general and does not tie prevalence to the dominant vendors. Most of the workarounds it describes are clinical-workflow coping. It does not quantify spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping caused by an aging core. The rest of the evidence is anecdotal or regional: Selayang going manual after a crash, Vietnam running paper and electronic records in parallel, and manual matching in Indonesia. The PMC page was CAPTCHA-blocked, so I confirmed the review's scope only through PubMed search results.

s4.why: The only primary, quantified source is VA testimony (March 2023): about 70% of VA MUMPS programmers are retirement-eligible. That covers one system (VistA), which is already being retired. For the dominant vendors, Epic and Oracle Health, scarcity is real but comes from vendor-gated certification and demand from new installs, not a dying skill base. Epic trains new graduates in-house. The figures here come from recruiters, such as the claim of 15 open Epic roles per certified analyst, which is secondary marketing. I found no primary evidence of skill scarcity for MEDITECH, Cerner CCL or SAP IS-H.

reasons_to_stay: High switching cost. MEDITECH's 10-K example: a typical 150-bed hospital pays a $3M product fee plus a $1M implementation fee, then about $30K a month.
Patient-safety and go-live risk. VA paused rollout for 20 months, and 75% of surveyed users said the new system did not make them as efficient as possible (GAO-25-106874).
Program cost overruns. VA's EHR estimate went from about $10B to $37-50B life-cycle.
Data migration from decades of clinical records. VistA holds 15M+ lines of MUMPS code, and VA says modernizing would mean rewriting it almost from scratch.
Epic's network effects (Care Everywhere, MyChart) and the KLAS-ranked suite lock in large systems. Epic's share keeps rising.
Regulatory and certification requirements (ONC, NHS DSPT, Kemenkes PMK 24/2022 RME and SATUSEHAT integration) favour incumbent certified vendors.
Public-sector budget and procurement constraints. Malaysia MOH cites budget limits, Queensland's procurement was delayed by a conflict-of-interest probe, and Vietnam's small bidders under-deliver.
Retraining large clinical workforces and the downtime risk of a cutover.

SAP ECC 6.0 (2006) runs on the R/3 base that launched in 1992, and most ECC users have not moved off it: DSAG's 2025-26 survey has only 37% of German-speaking ECC users planning to reach S/4HANA by 2027. The mid-market lineages are older still. MAPICS/Infor XA dates from 1977 on IBM midrange, BPCS/Infor LX from the early 1980s on IBM i, JD Edwards World runs RPG on System/38 and AS/400, Baan/Infor LN dates from the 1980s-90s, QAD MFG/PRO from the mid-1980s in Progress 4GL, and Epicor Vantage/Vista from the 1990s client-server era. s2.why: The quantified evidence covers one vendor. In DSAG's survey (198 leaders, Dec 2025 to Jan 2026), 37% plan to switch from ECC to S/4HANA by end-2027, about half by 2030, and 4% by 2033. SAP has extended ECC support to 2027, then 2030 at a premium, then a 2033 private-edition option. So the SAP programmes do run for years. Across ERP in general, Panorama's 2024 ERP Report gives a 15.5-month median project and says more than half finished on schedule. That cuts against 'multi-year' for typical mid-market manufacturing replacements. No source shows 7+ year contracts. JDE E1 premier support to 2033 is a support horizon, not a contract term.

s3.why: Spreadsheet workarounds are plausible and widely reported, but the cited evidence is a vendor survey (Qlector) of a small sample of Slovenian manufacturers, in which 50% supplement ERP planning with Excel or paper. Other figures are vendor or analyst claims that blame missing MES coverage rather than legacy ERP: IoT Analytics says 54% of plants used pen and paper or spreadsheets in 2024, and Galorath says 96% use Excel for cost estimation. No large-sample primary source ties re-keying or screen-scraping to the dominant legacy ERP systems.

s4.why: There is a quantified primary survey, but it covers the platform rather than the category's dominant system. In Fortra's 2026 IBM i Marketplace Survey (n=315), 69% name IBM i skills a top concern, up from 60% in 2025 and ahead of security for the first time in nine years. The secondary LiminalArc report adds that 72% of IBM i developers are over 50. This applies to the IBM i/RPG installed base (Infor XA/LX, JDE World, BPCS), which is a mid-market slice. It also spans every industry, not only manufacturing. For SAP ECC, the dominant system, the only evidence is DSAG citing 'skills shortages', and those are S/4 migration skills, not scarce ECC/ABAP skills. ABAP talent is still relatively plentiful.

reasons_to_stay: Business process change is the top barrier to leaving ECC (49% of ASUG respondents). Customizations come second (44%) and organizational inertia third (37%).

Migration capacity is short. DSAG cites skills shortages, parallel transformation projects and budget limits as reasons to delay.
Deep shop-floor integration (MES, PLCs, EDI with OEM customers, quality and traceability records) makes cutover risky for plants that cannot stop production.
Sunk cost and stability: decades-old RPG/Progress systems work, and replacement implementations still have a median of 15.5 months (Panorama 2024).

Licence economics: Maximo perpetual-to-MAS trade-up and AppPoints credit existing spend if customers stay with IBM

s1.why: The installed GL systems that dominate the category all shipped before 2005 as on-prem client-server or midrange software: SAP R/3 (1992, ECC 6.0 in 2006 on the same lineage), Oracle EBS Financials (late 1980s), PeopleSoft, JD Edwards World on AS/400, Great Plains Dynamics (1993) and Hyperion Enterprise/HFM. Mid-market GL moves (GP to Business Central, or to newer AI GLs) are measured in months. Oracle's support dates to 2037 show vendors extending support, not how long replacement takes. s3.why: Spreadsheet-heavy close work is widely reported, but the quantified sources are vendor material: Ledge's benchmark (n=100, 94% use Excel in the close) and BlackLine's own 10-K, where BlackLine has a commercial interest. differentiator: More legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Centrelink ISIS runs on Model 204, first deployed 1972. That covers the largest payers in US, UK and AU, so the evidence is not tied to one vendor. One caveat: there is no evidence for the ASEAN and India cores (BPJS, VSS, SSO, SSS/GSIS, KWSP), and Cúram/Deloitte eligibility systems are newer client-server or Java builds.

s2.why: Primary, quantified evidence of multi-year replacement. NAO (Feb 2024) says Universal Credit migration will finish at least 6 years later than planned, with some of it running to 2028. Australia's WPIT was a 7-year program of about A$1.5B, and by June 2020 only 13% of ISIS had been decommissioned. The Model 204 licence ran on an 11-year deal (2003-2014). DWP's VME re-platforming took 2016-2021. GAO found 6 of 8 sampled states still mid-modernisation of UI as of Feb 2023.

s3.why: The strongest primary evidence covers a single system. NAO (Sept 2021) found DWP State Pension administration has 'limited automation'. Caseworkers review at least three systems and set prompts by hand, and this led to 134,000 underpayments and a manual review of about 273,000 cases. In the US, GAO only implies paper-based UI processes, citing a reduction in paper as a modernisation gain. The ANAO finding that ISIS business rules are undocumented is about missing documentation, not workarounds. No quantified source shows spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping across the dominant systems in several countries.

s4.why: Several primary audit bodies document the skills gap directly. GAO-25-107795 (government-wide, covering SSA among others) says COBOL/assembly have a dwindling pool of skilled people and agencies pay a premium for staff or contractors. GAO-23-105478 says most sampled states lacked staff with the necessary expertise for UI systems. SSA OIG (2012) recommended planning for the loss of COBOL programmers. Replacements have failed or slipped. Australia scrapped a A$191M entitlements engine in 2023 because it ran slower than Model 204. Universal Credit is at least 6 years late.
Errors in benefit payments are politically costly. Deloitte system rollouts brought backlogs (Kentucky: 50,000 cases, 600+ defects) and wrong notices (KFF Health News).

The old cores are stable and pay out at huge scale: DWP about USD 202B a year, ISIS about 62M transactions a day. Rehosting COBOL (DWP VME-R, DRV Baden-Württemberg, CPF BEACON) is often preferred to a rewrite.
Benefit rules change every year by statute, so agencies have to keep paying while they migrate, which forces long parallel running.
Procurement and funding cycles (federal matching funds, multi-year budgets) favour large incumbent integrators.

differentiator: The category is less locked than core banking or mainframe tax because the leading platforms run on mainstream Java or .NET stacks with vendor SaaS migration paths, few hard skills shortages, and 3-to-5-year contracts. s1.why: Several dominant installed cores are shown by primary sources to date from before 2005 and to run as on-prem client-server or midrange systems. The Connected Places Catapult study of UK planning software found Idox, which over 90% of UK councils use, set up as a local client on planners' machines with document management on a local server (it calls these 'legacy planning software'). San Diego's audit says its homegrown PTS was designed in the late 1990s and went live in 2001. NYC DOB calls BIS a mainframe. Branson runs Naviline on an AS/400 with DB2 and has done for 20 years. Tidemark dates to 1984 and Hansen to the 1980s. Caveat: the two leading US products, Tyler EnerGov (about 2002) and Accela Automation (early 2000s, web-based Java), are borderline on the 2005 cut-off and are not mainframe.

s2.why: Independent government audits across different vendors show multi-year replacements. California's BreEZe was proposed in 2009 at $28M, cost $96M by 2015 and covered only about half its 37 entities (State Auditor 2014-116). San Diego's move from PTS to Accela was due to go live in May 2017, slipped to February 2020, and its budget grew from $10.9M to $17.7M (City Auditor 19-011). NYC DOB NOW has been replacing the BIS mainframe in stages since about 2016 and the two still run side by side. Singapore runs CORENET X in parallel with CORENET 2.0 from 2H 2023. Caveat: the contract terms seen are 3 to 5 years, not 7 or more (Oxford's 3-year minimum, San Diego's 5-year Accela contract, Idox 3-year extensions). Small councils often switch in 12 to 18 months. The evidence comes from large jurisdictions.

s3.why: The Catapult sector study rests on interviews across the UK planning industry and covers the dominant installed base (Idox, Northgate/NEC). It reports that planners are 'forced' into manual workarounds such as copying and pasting between programmes. Planning officers manage cases in Excel sheets and manual lists instead of the system's tracking tool, and GIS data is re-keyed by hand. In the US the evidence is anecdotal. Richmond's auditor found elevator tracking done manually after the EnerGov rollout, and Branson builds its Naviline reports in Excel. It is strong for the UK and weaker for the US and ASEAN. It is qualitative and has no percentage figures.

s4.why: The only quantified source is generic to IBM i. Fortra's 2026 survey found 69% of IBM i shops name skills a top concern, but that applies only to the AS/400 slice of the base (Naviline/H.T.E.). San Diego's audit gives a primary anecdote of key-person risk: the City over-relied on the one PTS architect from the 1990s, and losing that institutional knowledge delayed the Accela migration. Most dominant platforms (Accela, Tyler EnerGov, Idox Uniform, NEC, Infor Pathway) run on mainstream Java, .NET or Oracle/SQL Server stacks. No source shows a scarcity of skills specific to permitting.

reasons_to_stay: Decades of permit, parcel and case history plus scanned documents sit in proprietary schemas. The Catapult report describes a UK council that judged retrieving its own data from a vendor too risky because of contract complexity, so it chose to upgrade and extend instead.
Tight integration with finance, utility billing, GIS and cashiering in integrated suites (Naviline, Pathway, Tyler). Replacing permitting alone breaks fee and parcel links.
Large replacement programmes have failed publicly: California's BreEZe went from $28M to $96M and covered about half its planned scope. This makes councils and boards risk-averse.
Statutory clocks, fee schedules and local code rules are configured into workflows over years, and must be rebuilt and re-validated.

Procurement and budget cycles: UK councils often roll Idox Uniform maintenance forward in 3-year extensions (e.g., Tameside 2024-27, Dartford 2025-28, per Contracts Finder search results) instead of re-platforming.
National mandates in ASEAN (OSS-RBA, CORENET X, eBPLS) set the agenda, so local agencies wait for central integration rather than buy independently.
Vendor evergreen maintenance models (e.g., Tyler includes upgrades in maintenance) lower the pressure to switch.

systems: US county recorder land-records systems: Tyler Technologies Eagle Recorder / EagleSoftware, Harris Recording Solutions OnCore (legacy, 2003) and Acclaim, Fidlar AVID/Laredo, Kofile, Catalis Official Records, Infocon County systems on IBM AS/400 (IBM i)

Queensland Automated Titles System (ATS, from 1994)
Landgate WA Smart Register (replaced 2015 to 2017 by NLR-T/Advara)
NSW LRS and Victoria SERV registries (privatised under 35- and 40-year concessions)
Singapore SLA INLIS (1998) and the Land Titles registry
India: Bhoomi (Karnataka, NIC, 1999-2001), state RoR systems under DILRMP, NGDRS e-registration
Indonesia ATR/BPN KKP (Komputerisasi Kegiatan Pertanahan): desktop, then Geo-KKP, then KKP-Web

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The register carries a state guarantee of title and is bound to local land law. That makes it more locked in than typical enterprise software: replacements need statutory change, decades-long concessions and bulk data migration. But the cores are mostly bespoke systems from around 2000 rather than COBOL, so the skills risk is lower than in banking or tax.

s1.why: Primary sources show that the main register in most in-scope jurisdictions was built before 2005 as an on-prem or mainframe system and is still running. Queensland's ATS went live in 1994 and the 2026 Titles QLD practice manual still describes it. Singapore's INLIS dates from 1998. Malaysia's SPTB was implemented from 1995 and e-Tanah has replaced it in only 10 states. Karnataka's Bhoomi dates from 1999-2001. HMLR's own blog says its register and 140M documents sit on the mainframe. Landgate's CEO said all 37 Torrens jurisdictions ran old systems built around 2000. Caveats: the US county market is split, with Kofile and Tyler hosted systems spreading and AS/400 county systems shown only by anecdote, and no source gives a core build year for Indonesia's KKP.

s2.why: Primary government sources show both very long contracts and multi-year replacements. Victoria signed a 40-year registry concession in 2018 (A$2.86bn) and NSW signed a 35-year concession from 2017. Malaysia announced e-Tanah in 2003 and now targets full Peninsular coverage only by 2030. HMLR's Local Land Charges migration has slipped to end-2028, and it started its transformation in 2018 knowing it would run legacy systems for years. The Philippines LTCP was awarded in 2000 and had not started 5 years later. The concessions cover running the registry, not only software, but they still lock in the platform for decades.

s3.why: There are workarounds, but each source covers only one registry or comes from a vendor. HMLR's Strategy 2025+ says most of its data is paper, scans or PDFs, and that spatial and text data sit in unconnected systems. A UiPath case study (vendor source) says HMLR used 10 RPA bots as a tactical bridge over legacy systems. Kofile, also a vendor source, describes US county staff hand-indexing documents and searching microfiche. Landeed's business is pulling together fragmented state portals in India. No source quantifies spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping across the main registry systems.

s4.why: No source ties a skills shortage to land registry systems. HMLR does not disclose the language its mainframe uses. The only support is general COBOL statistics (Route Fifty, 2023) and an unverified Erie County, PA AS/400 anecdote whose page did not open. Many registry cores are bespoke Java or .NET systems built around 2000, and those skills are not scarce. Searches for registry-specific skills scarcity found nothing.

reasons_to_stay: The register carries a state guarantee of title (for example, the NSW Torrens Assurance Fund), so integrity outranks speed. HMLR said this explicitly when it delayed LLC to 2028.
Long concession and BOO contracts (35-40 years in AU, BOO in PH) lock in the operator's platform.
Data migration is hard: paper, microfiche and scanned titles (25M in PH, 27M titles at HMLR) must be converted while transactions keep flowing.
Changing the register often needs a statutory amendment (Malaysia amended the National Land Code for SPTB; Queensland's Land Title Act 1994 created ATS).
Procurement is political and slow, with audit-body challenges (e.g. COA questions on the PH LTCP).
Systems are bespoke to local law. Landgate found no off-the-shelf product among about 37 Torrens jurisdictions.

Nucleus Software FinnOne / FinnOne Neo retail and SME lending (APAC, India)

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category is more legacy-locked than typical in US mortgage servicing, where one 1960s-era mainframe (MSP) holds 63% of first-lien loans with 5 to 7 year contracts. It is less locked in origination, where Encompass and newer LOS and lending platforms are already cloud-hosted and challengers (nCino, Lentra, Mambu) are winning share.

s1.why: The dominant US servicing core is a pre-2005 mainframe, and primary sources quantify it. Black Knight's FY2022 10-K puts MSP on 32.8M first-lien loans, 63% of the US market. PennyMac's SEC-filed complaint says MSP was 'first developed over 50 years ago' and runs on a mainframe with batch processing. ICE job posts confirm z/OS COBOL/CICS. Other dominant cores also predate 2005: Loan IQ (1990s, about 70% of syndicated loan volume by vendor claim), ACBS (early 1990s) and Encompass (client-server, early 2000s). Caveats: the complaint is a litigant's allegation, and the origination side (Encompass, and FinnOne rebuilt as Neo) is now cloud-hosted. The strength rests on servicing.

s2.why: The 10-K says contracts 'typically span five to seven years', below the 7+ threshold. Deferred conversion costs amortized over 5 to 10 years point to stickiness but do not measure replacement time. The FTC 2023 ICE/Black Knight complaint (para 129) calls LOS switching 'expensive, lengthy, and resource-intensive' but gives no duration. The figure is redacted. The multi-year replacements cited are single-firm cases: PennyMac's MSP replacement ran about 2011 to 2019 (its own complaint), and Newrez's move to Valon only starts in 2027. Lock-in is real, but no primary source quantifies multi-year replacement across the installed base.

s3.why: The evidence is anecdotal or about single firms. The CFPB's 2017 Ocwen suit alleges manual workarounds on an in-house platform (REALServicing), not a dominant vendor system. PennyMac says it built 150+ custom modules around MSP's functional gaps, but those are add-on software, not spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds, and the claim comes from a litigant. The only survey (Kani 2025 via kennek, 56% manual spreadsheet reconciliation) is secondary, UK-only and about reconciliation, not origination or servicing. No primary quantified source shows spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping on the dominant systems.

s4.why: The evidence is one vendor's job posts plus a generic mainframe statistic. ICE is hiring for MSP and requires 8+ years of z/OS COBOL/CICS, which shows the skill is needed but not that it is scarce. The 71% figure for understaffed mainframe teams (BizTech 2025) is a secondary, cross-industry survey, not specific to this category. Loan IQ, Encompass and FinnOne skills are niche but not shown to be scarce. Encompass administrators are common in US mortgage hiring.

reasons_to_stay: Contracts typically run 5 to 7 years, and conversion costs are amortized over 5 to 10 years (Black Knight FY2022 10-K)
Switching is 'a significant undertaking' with lengthy timelines. ICE itself estimated the first-year cost of switching LOS for a lender (FTC complaint).
Investor and regulator reporting (GSEs, Ginnie Mae, CFPB servicing rules) is already built into incumbent systems. A rebuild risks compliance errors, as the CFPB's Ocwen case shows.
Ecosystem lock-in: ancillary services (PPE, default, data) are integrated with the incumbent LOS or servicing system, and the FTC says assembling them is a barrier to entry
Network effects in syndicated lending: agent banks and the counterparties they serve are all on Loan IQ
Data conversion risk for millions of borrower accounts. Ocwen still had 15% of a ResCap transfer unverified 3 years later.
Big-bank migrations are multi-year programs (PennyMac 2011 to 2019; Newrez to Valon starting in 2027)

name: Custom COBOL and mainframe applications (cross-industry)
systems: IBM Z mainframes running z/OS (MVS lineage) with custom COBOL, PL/I and Assembler applications
IBM CICS Transaction Server (online transaction processing, released 1969)
IBM IMS (hierarchical DB/transaction manager, installed 1968)
IBM Db2 for z/OS and VSAM data files
JCL batch and 3270 'green screen' (TN3270) terminal front ends
Micro Focus (now Rocket Software) COBOL / Enterprise Server
Unisys ClearPath Forward (MCP, from Burroughs 1961; OS 2200)
Fujitsu mainframes (sales end FY2030, support end FY2035)
Broadcom (ex-CA Technologies) mainframe tooling (IDMS, Datacom, Endevor etc.)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise software category: the dominant stack (z/OS, CICS, IMS, COBOL) dates from the 1960s and holds decades of undocumented business rules, and the vendor still ships new hardware every year, so staying put is cheaper and less risky than migrating.

s1.why: The dominant installed stack is IBM Z running z/OS, CICS (released 1969), IMS (installed 1968) and Enterprise COBOL. Unisys MCP dates from 1961. GAO-25-107795, a primary audit, finds that the 11 most critical US federal legacy systems are 23 to 60 years old. Two Treasury systems among them run on COBOL and Assembly. This sign holds by definition for the category, and IBM's 2022 share-of-top-50-banks figures show the base is still in use.

s2.why: GAO's primary audit is quantified. Of 10 critical federal modernizations flagged in 2019, only 3 were done by Feb 2025. Two of the rest are 5 or more years out, one has no date, and HHS plans run to FY2035. Two of the 11 systems in the 2025 review had no modernization plan at all. The evidence is strongest for government. The private-sector proof is the CBA core replacement (about 5 years, over A$1B), which is one case. It stays strong because the GAO figures span several agencies, but it is close to the line for banks.

s3.why: The only non-vendor evidence is from the Bipartisan Policy Center, a think tank. It interviewed state officials about COBOL unemployment-insurance systems and found paper processes and manual data entry. That covers one government niche, not the dominant bank, insurer and telco base. Screen-scraping of 3270 terminals is real and common, but the evidence comes from RPA vendors (UiPath terminal activities). GAO-25-107795 does not document spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds. No quantified cross-industry source was found.

s4.why: GAO (primary, 2025) says Treasury's COBOL and Assembly systems depend on languages with 'a dwindling number of people available'. It also says agencies pay a premium for specialized staff. Industry surveys add numbers, though most are vendor-commissioned. A 2018 Forrester study found enterprises lost 23% of mainframe staff in 5 years and 63% of those roles stayed unfilled. A Micro Focus survey found 60% of COBOL users name hiring as their top challenge. A 2025 survey found 71% of mainframe teams understaffed. One caveat: scarcity is weaker in IN and PH, where offshore service firms (TCS, Infosys) train mainframe staff at scale.

reasons_to_stay: Proven reliability and throughput: IBM says z17 handles up to 24 trillion operations per second and mainframes process 87% of transactions (IBM Think).
Long, costly, risky rewrites. CBA's core replacement took 5 years and cost over A$1B. GAO warns that undocumented modernization plans raise the odds of cost overruns and project failure.
Business rules are embedded in undocumented code that nobody fully understands.
Gartner (cited by IBM) expects 75% of 'mainframe exit' vendors to pivot or exit by 2030, which makes exit look risky.
Vendors commit to long roadmaps: Unisys ClearPath Forward 2050 and IBM's annual z cycles.
Regulatory and operational risk of migrating core ledgers, payments and tax systems.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Hospital RCM is more locked in than typical enterprise software because billing shares one M-based database with the EHR, so replacing billing means replacing the EHR. But the dominant cores are still actively developed, and most of the manual pain comes from payer connectivity, not the cores' age.

s1.why: The installed base is measured and old. KLAS market share (via HealthSystemCIO, May 2026) puts Epic at 43.7% of US acute hospitals, Oracle Health/Cerner at 21.9% and MEDITECH at 14.7%, about 80% of US hospitals combined. All three cores shipped well before 2005 as on-prem or client-server systems: Epic Resolute in 1987 on Chronicles/M, MEDITECH MAGIC in 1982 and Client/Server in 1994 (Expanse only in 2018), and Cerner Millennium, Soarian and Invision in the 1980s to 2000s. Outside the US the picture is the same: SAP IS-H has run for over 30 years, HBCIS dates from the 1980s, and TrakCare sits on an M database. Caveats: the dates come from Wikipedia and FundingUniverse company histories, not vendor filings. Epic is actively developed and often hosted. Physician-practice billing (athenahealth, eClinicalWorks) is mostly cloud, so this grade applies to hospital RCM.

s2.why: The evidence is a set of public-sector cases, not a category-wide measure. NYC H+H spent $289M over five years on Epic revenue cycle (a Politico reprint). iTnews estimates about seven years to replace Queensland's HBCIS. DSAG says tendering an IS-H successor alone takes about two years. The VA's 10-year Oracle Cerner contract and the LA County and SF 10-year Epic contracts were seen only in search snippets or on blocked pages. No KLAS or survey data on implementation length or typical contract term was found. Replacement also usually means a full EHR replacement, so these timelines describe EHR programs more than billing alone. The sign is plausible and repeated, but anecdotal.

s3.why: The 2024 CAQH Index is a primary, industry-wide, quantified source. Only 35% of medical prior authorizations are fully electronic (X12 278). 39% go through web portals or IVR, which means re-keying, and 22% are fully manual (phone, fax, mail, email). CAQH sizes the remaining savings at about $20B. RCM is also a main market for RPA bots that scrape payer portals. Caveat: the re-keying is driven mostly by payer-side connectivity, not by the age of the provider's billing core. The UC Davis 'dummy appointment' workaround is one anecdote, and the Indonesian SIMRS/E-Klaim re-entry claim comes from a vendor blog.

s4.why: The only cited source is a trade opinion piece (Health IT Outcomes) calling MUMPS programmers a dying breed. It has no labor-market data. Epic skills are scarce mainly because Epic gates certification behind employer sponsorship, not because the skill base is shrinking. Billing analyst roles themselves are configuration work, not M coding. No source quantifies an SAP IS-H/ABAP skills shortage. Surveys do report RCM staffing shortages (for example 63% of providers), but those are about coders and billers, not skills for a legacy system. The sign is plausible but not shown.

reasons_to_stay: Billing is tied into the EHR. Epic Resolute and MEDITECH financials share one database with scheduling and clinical data, so replacing billing usually means replacing the EHR.
Cash-flow risk at go-live. After the UC Davis Epic conversion, staff resorted to 'dummy' appointments to keep certain billing running.
Very high cost and long timelines: $289M over five years for NYC H+H revenue cycle, about 7 years and $200M+ for Queensland's PAS replacement.
Payer and regulatory rules are encoded over decades (US payer edits, German DRG billing in IS-H, BPJS INA-CBG, PhilHealth case rates). Rebuilding them is risky.
Vendors keep extending support. SAP IS-H has extended maintenance to 2030 and a transition option to 2033. Queensland bought extended HBCIS support to 2023.
Procurement friction. DSAG estimates two years just to tender an IS-H successor, and public buyers must run formal tenders.
Incumbent consolidation keeps customers in place. Oracle is folding Soarian and Invision into RevElate, IKS Health bought TruBridge, and MEDITECH reports 84% legacy retention.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Mortgage servicing is more legacy-locked than a typical enterprise software category because one vendor-hosted COBOL/CICS mainframe system (ICE MSP) runs roughly half or more of US mortgage loans, and network effects across subservicers, MSR transfers and GSE reporting make leaving costly. That lock-in is mostly a US phenomenon: elsewhere servicing sits inside general core-banking or lending suites.

s1.why: The dominant US system is ICE (formerly Black Knight) MSP. Black Knight's FY2022 10-K, a primary and quantified source, puts it at about 36M active loans against a US market of about 66M first and second liens and lines of credit. ICE's own 2026 MSP job post asks for z/OS COBOL batch, CICS, JCL and DB2/VSAM, which confirms the mainframe stack independently of PennyMac's partisan '50-year-old mainframe' claim. The 10-K itself only calls MSP 'a SaaS solution' and does not describe the technology. Outside the US the evidence is weak: Phoebus (UK, 1989) has no share data, and no specific pre-2005 servicing core was tied to the SE Asian regions. The strong grade rests on US dominance only.

s2.why: The evidence does not meet the 7+ year or multi-year bar for the dominant system. The FY2019 10-K figure is '12 to 18 months, or longer' to switch, which is not multi-year, and the FY2022 10-K only says 'long-term contracts' with no length. Published MSP renewals are 5 years (Cenlar, EverBank). The one 7-year term found is Mr. Cooper's commitment to Sagent, a single deal reported in trade press. A 7-year LoanCare renewal on MSP appeared in search results but was not verified. PennyMac's multi-year, module-by-module exit is one partisan case. The lock-in is real (30-year client tenures such as Cenlar), but neither duration test is shown directly.

s3.why: The evidence is indirect, and the main source is a litigant. PennyMac says it built 'hundreds' of bolt-on modules around MSP and that data is downloaded from and uploaded back to MSP. CFPB Supervisory Highlights Issue 11 (2016) found IT staff manually overriding data fields during servicing transfers, which is a transfer-specific finding. No primary or quantified source shows spreadsheets, re-keying or screen-scraping as routine practice across MSP or other servicing users.

s4.why: The only evidence specific to this category is one ICE job post for the MSP team. It asks for 8+ years of z/OS COBOL/CICS and treats AI coding tools as a plus, which suggests scarcity but does not quantify it. The Deloitte survey cited by BizTech (71% of firms say mainframe teams are understaffed) covers financial services in general, not mortgage servicing. No mortgage-specific vacancy, wage or retirement data was found.

reasons_to_stay: Switching takes 12 to 18 months or longer, and the cost is significant (Black Knight FY2019 10-K).
Regulators expect extensive testing and validation before a servicer changes major systems (PennyMac complaint).
Servicing transfers carry CFPB exposure: lost loss-mitigation documents and late payment crediting during data moves.
Investor, GSE and agency reporting (Fannie, Freddie, Ginnie, FHA/VA) is already built and certified on the incumbent.
Multi-year contracts (for example Mr. Cooper's 7-year commitment to Sagent) and long renewals lock buyers in.
Network effects: subservicers, MSR buyers and vendors integrate to MSP formats, so leaving it adds friction on every transfer.
Vendor litigation risk: Black Knight sued PennyMac in 2019 when it left MSP.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Payroll is more locked-in than typical enterprise software at the deep end: statutory tax, award and union rules are hard-coded, errors are not tolerated, and the evidence shows multi-year, billion-dollar public-sector replacements. It is less locked-in at the top and the bottom, where Workday (65%+ of the Fortune 500) and SaaS bureaus such as ADP RUN and Gusto already hold much of the installed base.

s1.why: First-ship dates are solid. SAP R/3 HR shipped in 1992, PeopleSoft HRMS in 1989, Lawson started as mainframe software, and California's payroll is a mainframe set of 12 systems, some nearly 50 years old. SAP's cloud Employee Central Payroll still runs the old SAP HCM payroll engine. But no source puts a number on the installed-base share of these cores. The one quantified share figure points the other way: Workday's 10-K says it serves 65%+ of the Fortune 500 on a core first shipped after 2005. US SMB payroll is mostly SaaS or bureau (ADP RUN, Gusto). So pre-2005 cores dominate public sector, higher education and part of mid-to-large enterprise, but not the category as a whole.

s2.why: Two separate primary, quantified cases on different stacks. (1) California LAO: the CSPS replacement costs about $1.2bn, takes about 6 years and completes Sept 2031. It follows the 21st Century/MyCalPAYS attempt, which began in 2004 and was suspended in 2013 after nearly a decade. (2) NHS England and Wales: the Oracle EBS-based ESR, which pays 1.9m staff, moves to a 15-year, GBP 1.4bn (inc. VAT) Infosys contract, and ESR support runs to 2035. SAP HCM extended maintenance to 2030 and H4S4 to 2040 extend the timeline further. Caveat: the quantified evidence is all public sector. Private-enterprise replacements are usually 12-36 months.

s3.why: The primary evidence is one 2013 municipal audit (Killeen TX): paper timecards are re-keyed into an AS400 and every check is recalculated in Excel. The better quantified source is the EY-PayrollOrg Payroll Pulse Survey (2022-23): 40% use SQL-fed spreadsheets and 18% manual processes as their primary way of working with payroll data. That covers data and reporting work, not core processing, and the survey does not tie it to legacy cores. Cloud payroll users report the same habit. The 51% spreadsheet figure is a vendor-cited poll (Strada/Alight).

s4.why: The only primary evidence is California LAO Report 3590 (2017), where the State Controller reports trouble hiring mainframe staff for the payroll system covering about 260k employees. The 2025 LAO CSPS report does not repeat this. InfoWorld (2008) is secondary. Nothing shows scarce SAP HCM, PeopleSoft or Lawson skills, which make up most of the installed base, or any skills gap in APAC or India. SAP HCM consultants are still abundant, and the market is moving toward SuccessFactors ECP.

reasons_to_stay: Payroll is mission-critical and has zero tolerance for error. Queensland Health's 2010 SAP payroll go-live underpaid or failed to pay about 78,000 staff and cost about AUD 1.2bn, which makes buyers very risk-averse.
Deep local statutory logic (tax, social security, awards and union agreements, e.g. PPh 21/BPJS in Indonesia, Australian awards) is embedded and tested in the old system.
Vendors keep extending support (SAP HCM to 2030 and H4S4 to 2040; PeopleSoft rolling to at least 2036), which removes any forcing deadline.
Replacement is a reimplementation, not an upgrade (e.g. Kronos WFC to UKG Pro WFM), and needs parallel payroll runs and data migration.
Public-sector procurement cycles and long managed-service contracts (NHS ESR: 15 years) lock incumbents in.
Integration with GL, time and attendance, pensions and benefits, and banks.

differentiator: More locked-in than a typical enterprise category. Decades of member benefit history and statutory rules must be migrated exactly, and many dominant buyers are single government funds, so replacement takes 5 to 15 years. Australia's super market is the exception: post-2010 platforms and frequent fund mergers make it less locked-in.

s1.why: FIS Omni/Relius is the dominant US DC recordkeeping engine (650 clients, 68m participants). The vendor's own retirement lead says it was built in COBOL more than 30 years ago and is only being rebuilt for cloud in 2026. Public plans show the same pattern in their own releases: Washington DRS was replacing a 30-year-old system in 2023, Massachusetts SRB a 38-year-old one in 2010, NY MEBEL ran on z/OS, and CalSTRS used its legacy system until 2025. Caveats: Australia's leading core (Bravura Sonata, launched 2010) is after 2005, and the UK's Altair has no disclosed first-ship date. So this is strong for the US and public sector, and less certain for AU and UK.

s2.why: Several primary agency sources each quantify a long replacement. CalSTRS's Pension Solution started pre-implementation in 2010, got budget approval in 2014 and went live in September 2025, with a $523m budget plus $105m post-go-live. Washington DRS signed a 4-year implementation plus 2 years of support with Sagitec (2023). EPFO's CITES 2.01 was approved in 2021 and went live in July 2026. FIS's own Omni rebuild took 4 years. Capita seeks 5 to 10 year TPA terms. Multi-year replacement is the norm across the dominant buyers.

s3.why: The direct evidence is vendor-authored. Sagitec's TRS case study describes re-keying across systems and employers sending data on paper or disk, and Aware Super's 'paper-based legacy systems' quote is also vendor-adjacent. UK industry material (TPR record-keeping research and PASA, both reported second-hand) says about a third of schemes keep non-digital records and that data gathering and calculations are manual. That points to paper and archive records, not quantified spreadsheet or screen-scraping workarounds on top of the dominant platforms. Plausible, but not primary or quantified.

s4.why: The main citation is a single 2013 Computerworld article about one system (NY MEBEL). The audit behind it came from NY DFS and the Comptroller disputed it. COBOL, CICS, DB2 and OmniScript skills for FIS OmniPlus appear in job and CV listings, but no source quantifies a shortage. Nothing was found for UK, AU or Asian provident funds. Dated and anecdotal.

reasons_to_stay: Benefit rules span decades of legislative changes and member history (DB accrual, tranches, transitional protections) that must be migrated exactly. HESTA moved more than a decade of data and still had a members-locked-out cutover period
Regulatory and fiduciary risk: payment errors to retirees are highly visible, and boards prefer incumbent stability
Long outsourcing and TPA contracts (Capita seeks 5 to 10 years) bundle software and administration
Challenger financial fragility: GROW Inc carried going-concern audit doubts and needed client debt and equity support before MUFG agreed to acquire it in 2026
Big-bang regulatory deadlines (Dutch Wtp by 2028, UK pensions dashboards) push funds to extend incumbents rather than switch mid-reform
Concentrated incumbent ecosystems (Heywood Altair across LGPS, FIS Omni across US recordkeepers) supply frameworks, interfaces and skilled staff
Fund mergers (AU consolidation from 1,656 to 771 APRA funds in 5 years) often settle on the acquirer's existing platform instead of a new one

name: Port and container terminal operating systems (TOS)
systems: Navis SPARCS / SPARCS Express (Kaleris), on-prem predecessor of N4
Navis N4 (Kaleris), first site live 2006
PSA CITOS (in-house, 1988)
Hutchison Ports nGen (in-house, 2003)
Tideworks Mainsail / Mainsail Vanguard (SSA Marine subsidiary)
Total Soft Bank CATOS (Korea)
RBS TOPS / TOPX (Australia)
Pelindo legacy TOS / PTOS-M being consolidated onto ILCS TOS Nusantara (Indonesia)
Operator in-house legacy TOS (for example Patrick Terminals' 30-year in-house system replaced by N4 in 2020; seen only in search snippets)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. A TOS is real-time control of cranes, gates and automated equipment, so cutovers need operational shutdowns and cores run 20 to 30 years. It is less locked than mainframe categories, because the dominant product (Navis N4, 2006) is a vendor-supported Java platform that gets regular upgrades and is moving to cloud.

s1.why: The market's dominant lineages began as on-prem client-server systems before or around 2005. PSA CITOS dates from 1988 and Navis SPARCS from 1989 (academic history). Hutchison nGen went live in 2003, RBS TOPX shipped in 1996, and Tideworks Mainsail launched in 1999. Primary customer sources confirm long-lived pre-2005 cores in production. GPA ran SPARCS/Express at Garden City from fall 2000 until its N4 cutover in April 2022. Patrick's CIO described replacing a '30-year-old legacy TOS' with N4 in 2020. Two caveats. The market leader, Navis N4 (389 terminals in GPA's FAQ, 500+ Navis ports per Kaleris), first went live in 2006, so it is a mid-2000s Java client-server rewrite rather than mainframe or midrange. No source documents mainframe or midrange architecture anywhere in this category.

s2.why: Primary operator sources show decades of tenure and multi-year replacement programmes at the largest operators. GPA ran SPARCS/Express for about 21 years (2000 to 2022). Patrick ran an in-house TOS for about 30 years. APM Terminals set a target to standardise its global portfolio on N4 by end-2021, but Aarhus only went live in March 2022, after data-migration problems that raised truck turn times. DP World Australia's consolidation of 19 systems onto N4 ran over several years. Single-site projects take 12 to 24 months, but that figure comes only from a vendor (INTECH). Contract lengths of 7+ years are not directly documented. The evidence is tenure and programme duration.

s3.why: The best quantified evidence is a global Tideworks survey with no stated sample size or year. In it, 89% of terminals use a TOS, yet 56% still rely on email and spreadsheets, only 33% use APIs, and 45%+ report integration problems with partners. That is vendor marketing, and it describes manual coordination around the TOS with partners, not re-keying or screen-scraping of the TOS itself. Portwise, a consultancy blog, says small terminals plan berths on spreadsheets or whiteboards. No independent or primary source quantifies workarounds at the large N4, CITOS or nGen sites.

s4.why: All of the scarcity evidence comes from one recruiter, KiTalent, across content-marketing pieces on Rijeka, Genoa and Sohar. They claim 8 to 11 months to hire senior N4 specialists, an N4 vacancy left open for about 11 months, and roughly 200 to 250 Navis/Kalmar automation engineers in the whole GCC. These pieces are unverified and possibly templated. The scarcity they describe is vendor-specific configuration know-how for a current product (N4, Java/Groovy), not a dying language or platform. No APAC, US or independent labour-market data was found.

reasons_to_stay: A TOS is mission-critical real-time control. Failed cutovers hurt operations badly: Felixstowe's June 2018 switch from Navis to Hutchison nGen caused lost boxes and truck queues of up to 16 hours (seen in search snippets; the Seatrade article returned 403).
Cutovers need a full operational shutdown window (GPA stopped operations overnight for N4) and 12 to 24 months of implementation.

Deep integration with automated equipment, gates, RFID, EDI and port community systems (PD Ports' Navis role lists SPARCS, MCP, Fast gate, WhereNet RFID, Camco Autogate, VBS). Every interface has to be re-done.
Data migration of 10+ years of container, vessel and customer history takes 4 to 8 months.
Big operators treat their in-house TOS as a competitive asset (PSA CITOS, Hutchison nGen) and build the next generation in-house rather than buy.
There is a small, concentrated vendor field, and specialist TOS staff are hard to hire. Both raise switching risk.

Oracle E-Business Suite (Oracle Applications / Financials: Purchasing, iProcurement, Payables), on-prem
JD Edwards World (RPG on IBM System/3x, AS/400 / IBM i) Accounts Payable and Procurement
JD Edwards EnterpriseOne and PeopleSoft Financials/Supply Chain (Oracle-owned on-prem)
Ariba Buyer (on-prem e-procurement, 1996-era), now SAP Ariba

Excel spreadsheets and paper/PDF invoice keying layered on top of the ERP
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more locked in than typical enterprise software at the core, because purchasing and AP sit inside the ERP system of record (SAP ECC, Oracle EBS) and replacing them takes years. It is less locked in at the edges, because cloud P2P and AP-automation overlays bolt on easily and the clerk-level skills stay plentiful.

s1.why: The dominant enterprise purchasing and payables core is SAP ECC MM/FI-AP. Its R/3 base shipped in 1992 as three-tier client/server, and R/2 dates from 1979 on mainframe. Gartner counts about 35,000 ECC customers worldwide and finds 61% had not licensed S/4HANA by end-Q4 2024, so most of the installed base still runs the pre-2005 core. Oracle EBS (late 1980s) and JD Edwards World (RPG on AS/400) add to this, though no install counts were found for them. One caveat: mid-market and SMB AP is moving to cloud (NetSuite, QuickBooks Online, Coupa), so this grade holds for the enterprise segment only.

s2.why: In 2020 SAP moved the Business Suite 7 deadline to end-2027, with paid extended maintenance to 2030, because of 'longer conversion phases' (primary). An ISG survey of 200 large firms found nearly 60% of SAP migrations run late and over budget. Gartner/ISG figures show 61% of ECC customers had not licensed S/4 eight years after the deadline was first announced. Birmingham City Council's SAP R/3 to Oracle replacement for finance and procurement started in 2018 and was still incomplete in 2026. All of this evidence is about the ERP as a whole, not P2P specifically. Bolt-on cloud P2P tools such as Coupa deploy in months, but the system of record underneath them is still slow to replace.

s3.why: Manual invoice keying is real and quantified. Ardent's 2025 ePayables survey (n=204, vendor-sponsored by Bottomline) found 48.6% of invoices arrive non-electronically and only 35.4% go straight through. But the cause is suppliers sending paper and PDF invoices, and the survey covers AP teams on every kind of system, including modern cloud ones. It does not tie re-keying or spreadsheet workarounds to the legacy ERP cores. Birmingham's GBP 5M of manual workaround labour is a single anecdote, and it comes from the replacement system failing, not the legacy one.

s4.why: The only quantified scarcity evidence covers the IBM i/RPG slice: Fortra 2026 found 69% name IBM i skills a top concern. That slice (JD Edwards World and homegrown AS/400 AP) is a minority of the installed base. For the dominant systems, SAP ECC and Oracle EBS, ABAP, MM and FI-AP consultants and AP clerks are widely available in every region in scope. The SAP skills-shortage surveys (for example UKISUG, 63%) measure S/4HANA migration skills, not scarcity of skills to run the legacy system. Tally, MISA and Accurate skills are abundant among SMB accountants.

reasons_to_stay: The ERP is the system of record for the general ledger, vendor master and 3-way match. Ripping out purchasing/AP means touching the core ERP, and Birmingham's SAP R/3 replacement shows what that risk costs.

Vendors keep extending support: SAP maintenance runs to 2027, optional to 2030, then customer-specific. Oracle extended EBS 12.2 Premier Support repeatedly (per search results, through at least 2036/2037). That removes any forcing deadline.
Heavy customisation (ABAP, RPG, Oracle Forms) encodes approval rules, tax and local e-invoicing compliance.
Bolt-on AP automation (capture, workflow) can be layered on top without replacing the core.
SMBs in IN, ID, VN rely on local tax/e-invoice compliance built into Tally, Accurate and MISA, and accountants are trained on them.
Migration is multi-year, scarce SI capacity goes to S/4HANA conversions, and finance teams fear period-close disruption.
